KEY MESSAGE 1... 
New model data continues to reinforce flash flooding as the
primary threat for tomorrow with QPF estimates near 3-4 inches
in spots. Severe threat will be dependent on heating but remains
and looks to favor areas west of our heavy rain tomorrow 
afternoon. 

Flash flooding:
A plume of high PWATS (in excess of 2.00" and near the daily
max) will overspread most of the region overnight into Sunday
with high confidence. Meanwhile, the vertically stacked cyclone
allows for southerly wind flow parallel to the baroclinic zone,
setting the stage for training. 

Rainfall surges northeastward into western PA overnight riding 
along warm advection. This rain looks to be low to moderate in 
intensity and lacks a high likelihood of flood risks itself but
could prime locations for high water issues later in the day. 
There is likely a small break between morning shower activity 
decaying and the pickup of more sustained storms tomorrow 
afternoon. 

Warm rainfall processes will be efficient with freezing levels 
north of 12-13 kft. Three hour flash flood guidance (FFG) across
the region is near 2 inches owing to our recent dry stretch. 
One hour FFG values across much of the region are near 1.50 
inches but those in urban centers still remain close to an inch.
Probabilities of rainfall rates greater than 1.5"/hr peak near 
30% across portions of the region and suggest 1-hr FFG may not 
be reached by any single storm (except in urban centers). This 
would point our flash flood threat towards requiring multiple 
rounds of storms crossing the same area targeting our 3-hr FFG 
values instead.

HREF and REFS 95th percentiles favor isolated pockets of 3-4
inches of rainfall in 6 hours tomorrow afternoon. While exact
location remains a little fuzzy and likely could until the first
round of storms begin to fire, the most favored locations appear
to be NW PA and areas along the ridges that could be primed from
morning rain. Average return intervals highlight the potential 
to see a 10-20 year rain event at some locations across the
region tomorrow. Probabilities of 3" or more of rain in 24h 
from the HREF features several relative maxima, including an 
axis from YNG-FKL (probabilities of 60-70%) and from MGW-AOO 
(probabilities of 60-80%). A short fuse Flash Flood Watch may be
needed across the region to highlight these risk areas. 

Severe thunderstorms:
Model trends continue to suggest less-favorable shear profiles
for potential weak tornadoes given largely straight-line
hodographs and low SRH and 0-1km shear values across much of the
area. However, probabilities of STP values >1 and localized
areas of enhanced low level curvature in model hodographs do
seem to exist in NE OH along the surging warm front and tucked
up against the eastern ridges. Tornadic activity tonight in a
similar airmass and setup across far western OH showed
distinctly different and far better hodographs for TOR
development. Sampled 12z and ACARS soundings across the region
tomorrow will go a long way to flesh out our TOR risk Sunday. 
At this time, it still remains possible to see a brief weak 
tornado or two but this threat could wax or wane depending on 
data we receive overnight and early tomorrow morning.

Nonetheless, a damaging wind threat does exist given 30-35 
knots of deep- layer shear, MLCAPE around 1300 J/kg and model 
soundings suggesting DCAPE values near 1000 J/kg. All of these 
and our high PWATs suggest water loaded downbursts could occur. 
The coverage/intensity of storms depends on how much heating we
observe tomorrow. Looking upstream over parts of IND ad KY 
where the dry slot allowed for breaks in the clouds, 
extrapolation brings that across eastern Ohio and possibly into 
northern WV and western PA Sunday afternoon. Model depictions of
the event show this as well with heavy rain focused further 
east and storms firing in eastern Ohio and moving north along 
with the surging warm front. Either way, breaks in clouds and 
rain will likely play a large role in storm intensity tomorrow 
afternoon. 

Machine learning is mostly in line with SPC with Nadocast 
putting a 15% chance of severe wind over western PA and the 
northern WV Panhandle and evening hinting at low end tornado
probabilities in NE OH. Many pieces still need to fall in line
for severe weather to occur, but several key ingredients look
like they could locally come together. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
The slow-moving upper-level low finally kicks out of here mid 
week, quickly followed by broad troughing across the Great Lakes.
This spells continued chances of showers and thunderstorms 
through next week. Shower and storm probabilities will coincide
with the afternoon peak heating hours. Despite near daily
chances, some locations may not see a drop of rain and even in
locations where it does rain, long stretches of dry weather are
expected. There will be periods of sunshine as well, so don't 
put away the sunglasses just because you see a chance of rain in
